name: Buddhiyoga, the yoga of understanding (BhG 2.39–53)
method_summary: Hold the understanding 'according to yoga' in acting (2.39): a single, resolute understanding (2.41); take refuge in understanding rather than making the fruit the motive (2.49); be the same in success and failure — equanimity is yoga, and yoga is skill in actions (2.48, 2.50); let the understanding cross the thicket of delusion and stand immovable in samādhi (2.52–53).

warnings.text: Those attached to enjoyment and power, carried away by the flowery speech of the Veda-delighters, do not have resolute understanding in samādhi (2.42–44).
The understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless (2.41).
The understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
For those attached to enjoyment and lordship, carried away by the flowery speech of the ritual-minded, resolute understanding is not established in samādhi.
Wretched are those whose motive is the fruit.

stage: all; culminates in understanding immovable in samādhi (2.53)
signs_of_progress: No effort is lost and even a little protects from great fear (2.40); casting off good and evil deeds (2.50); freedom from the bondage of birth (2.51); nirveda towards what is heard (2.52); attaining yoga (2.53).

name: Slaying desire, the enemy
method_summary: First restrain the senses and slay desire, the destroyer of knowledge and discernment (3.41); knowing that which is beyond the understanding, steady the self by the self and slay the enemy in the form of desire (3.43). Desire's seat is the senses, mind and understanding (3.40).

warnings.text: Desire is an insatiable fire, the constant enemy of the knower, covering knowledge.
The enemy in the form of desire is hard to overcome (durāsada).

name: Restraint and withdrawal of the senses (indriya-saṃyama)
method_summary: Withdraw the senses from their objects on all sides as a tortoise draws in its limbs (2.58); restraining them all, sit yoked, intent on Kṛṣṇa (2.61); keep the senses withheld from their objects on all sides (2.68); move among objects with senses free of attraction and aversion and under the self's control (2.64); control the senses by the mind while acting (3.7); restrain the senses first in order to slay desire (3.41).
signs_of_progress: serenity (prasāda), the end of all sorrows and steady understanding (2.64–65)
even the inner taste for objects turns away on seeing the highest (2.59)

warnings.text: For one who abstains, the objects turn away but the taste (rasa) remains; it turns away only on seeing the highest.
The turbulent senses forcibly carry off the mind even of a discerning person who strives.
The mind that follows the roving senses carries off wisdom as the wind a ship on the water.
Restraining the organs of action while dwelling on objects in the mind is hypocrisy (mithyācāra).
Beings follow their nature; 'what will restraint accomplish?'
Attraction and aversion lie in the object of each sense; do not come under their sway, for they are waylayers.
The turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind even of a wise man who strives (2.60); the mind following the roving senses carries away wisdom like wind a ship (2.67).
Restraining the organs of action while recalling objects in the mind is hypocrisy (3.6); beings follow their nature — what will suppression achieve? (3.33).

equivalents.note: The Gītā's withdrawal of the senses from their objects (tortoise image); the word pratyāhāra is not used in ch. 1–3.

notes: Merger: probably the same as the skeleton's prc:indriya-nigraha ('Restraint and withdrawal of the senses', BhG 2.58, 3.41); both extractors used this id, so it is kept; flagged for the de-duplication pass.

name: Resigning all actions to the Lord (mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi saṃnyasya)
method_summary: Renouncing all actions in Kṛṣṇa, with a mind directed to the self, free of expectation and of 'mine', and with the fever gone, act (fight) (3.30); those who follow this teaching constantly, with faith and without carping, are freed from actions (3.31).

warnings.text: Those who carp at this teaching and do not follow it are deluded about all knowledge and lost (3.32).
Those who cavil at this teaching and do not follow it are deluded in all knowledge and lost.

name: Karma-yoga, the yoga of action
method_summary: Undertake action with the organs of action, the senses controlled by the mind, without attachment (3.7); do the prescribed action, since action is better than inaction (3.8); act for the sake of sacrifice, free from attachment (3.9); keep one's entitlement to the action and not to its fruit, the fruit not being the motive (2.47); act established in yoga, the same in success and failure (2.48); act, as the knower does, for holding the world together (3.20, 3.25).

warnings.text: One should not be attached to inaction (2.47); outward restraint of the organs of action while dwelling on objects in the mind is hypocrisy (3.6).
Action other than for the sake of sacrifice binds the world (3.9).
Do not let your attachment be to inaction.
Actionlessness is not attained by not undertaking actions, nor perfection by renunciation alone.
Restraining the organs of action while the mind dwells on sense-objects is hypocrisy (mithyācāra).
The wise should not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action.

signs_of_progress: Casting off good and evil deeds (2.50); freedom from the bondage of action and of birth (2.39, 2.51, 3.9); attaining the highest and perfection (3.19–20).
prerequisites: control of the senses by the mind (3.7)
understanding that is resolute and single (2.41)

name: Offering rice-balls and water to the ancestors (piṇḍodaka-kriyā)
method_summary: Mentioned only: Arjuna says that when a family's classes are mixed its ancestors fall, deprived of the rites of offering rice-balls and water (1.42). The chunk gives no procedure.

name: Cultivating sameness (samatva)
method_summary: Make pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same, and then act (2.38); be the same in success and failure — this sameness is called yoga (2.48); the steadfast person whom these do not disturb, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality (2.15).
signs_of_progress: not disturbed by pleasure and pain (2.15)
neither rejoicing nor hating on meeting the pleasant or the unpleasant (2.57)

name: Performing one's own dharma (svadharma)
method_summary: Look to one's own dharma and do not waver: for a kṣatriya, fight a battle that accords with dharma (2.31); perform one's own dharma even if imperfectly rather than another's well (3.35).

warnings.text: Abandoning one's own dharma incurs sin and disgrace (2.33–36); another's dharma brings fear (3.35).

name: Enduring the sense-contacts (titikṣā)
method_summary: The contacts of the senses give cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go and are impermanent — endure them (2.14). The one they do not disturb is fit for immortality (2.15).
prerequisites: seeing that the sense-contacts are impermanent (2.14)
signs_of_progress: not being disturbed by them; sameness in pleasure and pain (2.15)

name: Sacrifice and eating its remains (yajña, yajña-śiṣṭa)
method_summary: Summary as the text states it (no procedure is given): action done for the sake of sacrifice does not bind, so act for it free of attachment (3.9); by sacrifice nourish the gods, who nourish you in turn (3.10–11); offer to the gods what they give before enjoying it (3.12); eat the remains of sacrifice (3.13); keep the wheel of food, rain, sacrifice and action turning (3.14–16).
signs_of_progress: the highest good through mutual nourishment (3.11)

warnings.text: One who enjoys what the gods give without offering to them is a thief.
Those who cook only for their own sake eat sin.
One who does not keep the wheel turning, delighting in the senses, lives in vain.

One who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering to them is a thief (3.12); those who cook only for themselves eat sin (3.13); one who does not keep the wheel turning, delighting in the senses, lives in vain (3.16).

name: Eating the remainder of the sacrifice
method_summary: The good eat what remains of the sacrifice and are freed from all faults, whereas those who cook for their own sake eat sin (3.13).

warnings.text: Those who cook only for their own sake eat sin (3.13).
